title: Come, my beloved
hook: Shlomo Alkabetz's song greets Shabbat as a bride; everyone turns to the door at the end
tomorrow: A good thing to give thanks (Psalm 92:2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabbalat Shabbat, six psalms for six days. Your line was welcome the day. Did you step out and greet it? Today, the song at the center of that welcome. Day six hundred fifteen.

Picture a wedding. The music swells, and every head in the room turns toward the back, toward the doors, because the bride is about to walk in. Now picture a synagogue on Friday night. A song has been building, verse after verse. And at the last verse, the whole congregation stands, turns around, and faces the doors at the back. Some bow. Nobody walks in. Nobody needs to. The guest they're turning to greet is the Sabbath, arriving like a bride.
screen: `EVERY HEAD TURNS TO THE DOOR.` → `THE LAST VERSE.` → `NOBODY WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: Lecha dodi means come, my beloved. The refrain goes: come, my beloved, to meet the bride; let us welcome the face of Shabbat. It was written by Shlomo Halevi Alkabetz, one of the kabbalists of Safed, in the sixteenth century. He signed it, in a way. The first letters of the first eight verses spell his name, Shlomo Halevi. The words are made almost entirely of older words. Come, my beloved, comes from the Song of Songs. In the old Jewish translation: "Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field." And the bride comes from the Talmud, where a sage stood at sundown on Friday and said: come, O bride, come, O bride. Here's what surprises people. Most of the song isn't about Shabbat at all. The middle verses speak to Jerusalem, as if to a city lying in the dust. Shake off the dust, arise. Wake up, wake up, your light has come. It's a song of hope that the broken will be rebuilt, set inside the welcome of a single day. Then the final verse. Come in peace, crown of her husband, and it ends with that line from the Talmud: come, O bride, come, O bride. That's when everyone turns. In Safed they were facing the setting sun in the fields. Today they face the door. Lecha Dodi has been set to a great many melodies, and in many synagogues the tune changes with the seasons and the calendar.
screen: `COME, MY BELOVED, MEET THE BRIDE.` · `ALKABETZ SIGNED IT IN THE LETTERS.` · `WAKE UP, JERUSALEM.` · `COME, O BRIDE.` · then, large: `COME, MY BELOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face the door on the last verse. Stand, if you can. Settle, and breathe. Then turn around, slowly, and face the door of the room you're in. Picture something good about to come through it. Not a person you're waiting on. A day of rest, a quiet, a peace. If you know the words, say come, O bride, quietly. If not, just say come in. Bow a little, if you like. Then stay facing it. The bell holds the time.
Lecha dodi. Come, my beloved. The Safed song that greets Shabbat as a bride, and turns the whole room to the door.
Your line: come, my beloved. Today, when someone you love walks in the door, stop what you're doing and turn toward them. Day six hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Lecha Dodi is sung in the Friday evening service after the six psalms of Kabbalat Shabbat; at the last verse the congregation stands, turns to face the entrance, and many bow at 'come, O bride'. Mourners in their first week often enter at this point and are greeted.

fork.setup: you're in a synagogue on Friday night. Lecha Dodi reaches its last verse: come, O bride. what do you do?
options: stand, turn to face the door, and bow.
fork.reveal: everyone turns to face the door, greeting Shabbat the bride. in Safed they faced the setting sun.

original.note: Hebrew: come, my beloved, from Song of Songs 7:12.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty Friday night song.
what it means: a welcome for Shabbat as a bride, wrapped around a hope for Jerusalem's rebuilding.
what a scholar hears: Alkabetz's acrostic signature, Song of Songs 7:12, Rabbi Yannai's 'come, O bride' from Shabbat 119a, and Isaiah's language.

sources.quoted: Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field

notes: Song of Songs 7:12 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Shabbat 119a: Rabbi Yannai's 'bo'i chalah, bo'i chalah'; paraphrased.
Acrostic: the first eight stanzas spell Shlomo Halevi; there are nine stanzas; confirm.
Mourners entering during Lecha Dodi is a common Ashkenazi custom; confirm.
